ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
In football matches, the tactic of "breaking through the flanks and crossing from the byline" is often used, where an attacking player dribbles the ball along the sideline and crosses near the goal line. A football field is $100\mathrm{m}$ long and $55\mathrm{m}$ wide. An attacking player kicks the ball forward along the sideline, and the ball moves in a straight line at a speed of $14\mathrm{m/s}$ after passing the midfield line. The ball experiences a constant resistance equal to 0.2 times its weight. At the same time the ball passes the midfield line, a forward from the attacking team starts chasing the ball from point A, which is $1\mathrm{m}$ directly behind the ball, along the sideline. His starting process can be considered as a uniformly accelerated linear motion with an initial speed of zero and an acceleration of $2.5\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$, and he can reach a maximum speed of $10\mathrm{m/s}$. Both the player and the ball can be treated as point masses, and the gravitational acceleration is $g=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$.

1. Find the magnitude of the velocity of the football 2 seconds after it starts moving from the center line.
2. Determine whether the forward can successfully catch up with the ball. If possible, calculate the time required; if not, provide the reason. Do not add any additional content.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure is a schematic diagram of a rectangular football field, with the long side labeled as 100 m and the width on the right side labeled as 55 m; in the middle of the field there is a halfway line and a center circle, and it is labeled “mid”; near the halfway line, at the lower sideline, point A is marked, indicating that the forward starts from point A on the sideline, and the ball moves forward along the sideline. Reasoning: Take the position where the ball passes the halfway line as x=0, and take the direction along the sideline toward the opponent's goal as the positive direction; the forward is initially at x=-1 m. The resistance force on the football is 0.2 times its weight, so the magnitude of the deceleration is a=0.2g=0.2×10=2 m/s^2. Therefore the football's velocity is v_b=14-2t, and its position is x_b=14t-t^2. When t=2 s, v_b=14-2×2=10 m/s. The forward first undergoes uniformly accelerated motion with initial velocity 0 and acceleration 2.5 m/s^2, and the time needed to reach the maximum speed 10 m/s is 10/2.5=4 s. When t≤4 s, x_p=-1+0.5×2.5t^2=-1+1.25t^2. Let x_p=x_b, obtaining -1+1.25t^2=14t-t^2, that is, 2.25t^2-14t-1=0; its positive root is greater than 4 s, so he cannot catch up within the first 4 s. When t≥4 s, the forward moves uniformly at 10 m/s, and the position is x_p=-1+20+10(t-4)=10t-21. Let x_p=x_b, obtaining 10t-21=14t-t^2, that is, t^2-4t-21=0; solving gives t=7 s or t=-3 s, and taking the valid solution t=7 s. Therefore the forward can catch up with the football, taking 7 s.
